utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning to you, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the Case Number IT-03-68, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam, and good morning to you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and also good morning to my learned friends of the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I'm here together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers and Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends and colleagues. I am Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones I appear for Naser Oric. We have with us our legal assistant Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. Now, how are we going to go about this. I take it you had not actually finished because I cut you halfway or whichever part of the way it was. So I would suppose that you should continue, unless you want to hear any additional information that Mr. Di Fazio said he would be coming forward with this morning. It's up to you. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My suggestion to you would be to hear what he has to say in addition to what he said yesterday, and of course you have all the time you require to recapitulate on what you submitted yesterday and conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's probably best to proceed that way because we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I think, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We've had more documents disclosed to us on this subject and we might say, in terms of this whole issue, it's reaching the stage, I think, where at least we feel that it might be better to finish with this witness because there's no meaningful way that I can examine in chief or re-examine on these documents which we're receiving even last night and perhaps more will emerge. At this point we're increasingly thinking that it's best to finish with this witness and then to look at this issue later. We have another couple of preliminaries but as far as this is concerned we're happy to hear from Mr. Di Fazio and then respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So is there an agreement that we will leave it until the end after we've finished with the testimony of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, as far as I'm concerned I'm in Your Honours' hands on that. I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I think it's a more practical approach --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- because I have got ever interest to see if this witness goes first. If he has got an invalid or handicapped mother, I think we can't keep him here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, if that's the case, if Your Honours please, I'll excuse myself and tend to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, but make yourself -- keep yourself available on short notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll be available at short notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And I imagine it will be later -- Ms. Sellers might be able to give us a vague idea of how long she'll be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we hope that this will be the last time that we have an incident like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The only other matter is whether or not the examination-in-chief will be complete notwithstanding anything that's in the documents. Are we correct in making that assumption or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, if you want to volunteer information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, well, it's simply this: We reserve our position in terms of prejudice caused by not having these documents and our position really is that since we've already obviously proofing with the witness several days ago, that there is no meaningful way that we can make use of the documents we're receiving now. So that's why I'm -- I would conclude my examination-in-chief, as I've already done, but we reserve our position that the prejudice, even with regards to this witness, never mind other witnesses, remains with this disclosure of these documents because we can't make use of them on short notice. That's our position.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in that context, I can assure you, Mr. Jones, that when we come down with our decision we will address that in the most comprehensive manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I raise another issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's simply this: That we've been notified that the Prosecution intends to use an exhibit, P98.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I saw the list this morning but, to be honest with you, I had my secretary digging up these documents in my room and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I simply mention it now because in the interest of finishing expeditiously with this witness I have to say that for our part we can't see the possible relevance of that video with this witness and we certainly would maintain that nothing in my examination-in-chief gives rise to cross-examination on that document. And I mention it because if the Prosecution does wish to use that document, we'll have to have the witness out, we'll have to have arguments about it because we're certainly not going to just concede that they can use that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have to refresh our memory as to the part that the Prosecution -- apart from that video that the Prosecution wants to refer to and that will have to be done in the absence of the witness, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't recall from memory even what video this is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I could explain what video it is and certainly within the contents [sic] of the direct examination I believe that it has become pertinent from evidence that's been elicited on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can Mr. Di Fazio leave in the meantime? Mr. Di Fazio, you can go and continue your searches.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the video concerns prisoners that were held in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Simply, it's a video that has been shown before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but how does it tie up with the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not saying that every question on cross-examination necessarily has to be tied up with the examination-in-chief because the relevant Rule itself allows for more than that. But since this matter has been raised by Mr. Jones and he is claiming that it has got nothing to do with his direct and it is -- he is going to object to the -- to its use, perhaps it's the case of your explaining why you want to make use of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. The Defence elicited from Mr. Alic his opinion on atrocities that occurred with prisoners of war. They also elicited from Mr. Alic what did he believe should be done to persons who had committed such atrocities and implication of justice for the victim, direct questions, direct subjects that were brought up by Mr. Jones on direct examination, and I intend to just to review that area. I believe Mr. Alic is more than capable of giving his opinion on the similar situation. Now, I am quite surprised, as a matter of fact, to see that evidence that has been submitted, that has been deemed relevant and probative within the context of this trial is now being objected to because of a witness who has been presented. The Trial Chamber has seen this video, has certainly felt that it was relevant for the purposes presented and relevant to the counts within this document, and it is within this context that I intend to use it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones, do you want to react to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour, as I suspected the reasoning is weak to the point of being nonexistent. Firstly, for the last point Miss Sellers seems to be saying that, provided a document is an exhibit it's relevant for all purposes with all witnesses in any examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think she -- I don't think really she meant it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, that is what she said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Probably that way, yeah, but it may be understood that way for sure, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Of course we have to look at this witness, his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a legal heresy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And then as far as -- I really -- I hesitate to say this, but I really consider the Prosecution is trying to make -- is going to make a point that should there be justice where people have been mistreated, and it really comes down to something as trite as that when obviously Your Honours are not going to disagree with that proposition. Much more importantly, specifically, we -- I didn't ask this witness's opinion as an expert. He's not an expert, he's not here to give his opinion. The issue was: In the area of Fakovici were Serb, Serb volunteers, killing with impunity. And the point about impunity is that if there's no punishment it means that it can be widespread, and if it's widespread, killing of Muslims in the Fakovici area, it's a dangerous situation, and therefore Fakovici becomes a target, a military-justified target. That's a very specific purpose for which I was asking the question. I wasn't making a point about, Are Serbs are getting away with it? And now Miss Sellers is going to make the point, Well, shouldn't there be justice in the case of these people as well? That's just one point. I have a further couple of points to make in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's conclude on this one. Do you wish to submit --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I haven't quite finished Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: On this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, I'm sorry. I apologise to you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This witness is talking about Jagodnja and Joseva, talking about his area, and we're talking about someone committing crimes in that area. This is a prison in Srebrenica, it's got obviously nothing to do with this witness. He wasn't talking about a prison in Srebrenica, he wasn't talking about Srebrenica in 1992, which is what's concerned with in this video. And moreover, and we can -- if need be, I think we'll have to go into this. We can look at the evidence which has been given in relation to that video, which is in fact that -- and I'll quote from the transcript. It's Nedeljko Radic, Friday, 14th of January. When I cross-examined him about this video I established with him that actually the beatings which occurred after they'd left the prison and after they'd last seen or allegedly seen -- or been seen by our client, were very severe and, in fact, I'll quote: "And the beatings on the 16th of Sarac and Zoran were pretty severe, weren't they, from what you could tell. "Yes. "Weren't those beatings in fact worse than any beatings they'd received prior when they were detained in the SUP. "Yes, of course." Now, this video is showing people with marks on their face which on the evidence which has been given were sustained -- a great part of it were sustained after they'd -- allegedly after they had last been seen by our client. So, are we willing to -- are Your Honours really going to accept that for this witness, who is in Jagodnja and Joseva in 1992, it's relevant testimony for him to be shown a video of prisoners from not -- early 1993 and to establish with that the proposition that people should be punished for crimes. It comes to: That's the only point the Prosecution wants to make. And the danger -- the reason I react, Your Honour, is I don't think this trial should be hijacked to show videos of people with bruised faces to try and make some point, to try and impress Your Honours emotionally so that you'll the, I don't know, be turned against our client. That's totally inappropriate and it's -- well, I certainly think the Prosecution should be above that and I certainly think the Trial Chamber should not allow that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I certainly can agree with the Defence that the Prosecution is above that, the showing of lurid videos for the purpose of trying to make Your Honours not undertake the professional responsibility. Let there be no misunderstanding about that

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me assure you we have a much thicker skin than you think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So what's the relevance then? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll put to you a question. Obviously we will go out, leave the courtroom, for a couple of minutes to decide on this, the three of us, but my question is this: You want to elicit an answer, which you have already described, sort of, the nature of which you have already described, from the witness. Can't you put the question which would have the same effect of eliciting an answer from the witness, without the need of showing the video?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, if you put to the witness the proposition: If what happened to Muslims happened to Serbs, I -- you invert the position, you put the question. I don't think you need to necessarily show him the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could state two things preliminary to Defence's argument. First of all, factual basis that this occurred in 1992 during the time period that the witness is referring to, the crimes that were committed were committed not only in Srebrenica but within armed conflict in which we're saying the subordinates of Mr. Oric participated and -- and within the SUP, and in addition with Mr. Oric's subordinates outside of a jail cell of the SUP. So let's talk about in terms of the factual background. The other is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: About which he has not testified.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he has testified about attacks in 1992 in this region, he has testified about going to Srebrenica in 1993. I am not trying to say that he was either present in the SUP. I just want to clarify factually so I can get to the more important which Your Honour has posited. Second, factually, I believe that that's an issue that the Defence could have likewise just asked Mr. Alic: Do you think that people who have committed crimes that were described as killing of prisoners of war or people in reconnaissance, should they meet justice, that was done after reading a document and talked about snakes going around decapitated heads. If we're talking about simplicity and just wanting to elicit a simple issue of justice it was illustrated by the Defence in quite a different manner. Now, Your Honour, in abundance -- an abundance of respect for this Trial Chamber and of understanding that the Trial Chamber has seen evidence and understands it, and in certainly no way to elicit from Mr. Alic anything other than the essence of those questions that were germane to the one part of the direct examination, I am more than willing to either reduce the video to one or two still shots so that he can see that we are comparing situations in terms of abuse that might be within a similar realm. I would contend that the Defence, when they feel that a point must be illustrated by graphic material, the Prosecution has never objected to the graphic material when it has been shown to be relevant, whether they be autopsies or whether they be anything in relationship to the Defence's case. I must state also that this Trial Chamber has allowed the Prosecution, knowing when it's relevant on a limited basis, to also see such materials. When it is pertinent to the question and to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. indictment, we are very grateful for the Trial Chambers and for the Defence's allowing that it's relative and probative evidence. Now, because the Prosecution has understood that Your Honours do feel that the question in and of itself, the theme that first arose in the Defence's direct examination is relevant and probative and can be asked, could be asked, without showing a film, possibly a still shot, the Prosecution is more than willing to abide by any decision of Your Honours to put forward the question, see what answer is elicited by Mr. Alic, and if within your graces to show either a part or a still of a video. That certainly seems to be within the understanding of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I think firstly the Prosecution is proceeding from a complete misunderstanding of what my question was about. I wasn't saying: Should people be punished for war crimes, and obviously this witness isn't here as a legal expert or a moral expert or philosophical expert who we need his evidence whether the crime should be punished. That's why I say it's so ridiculous. We're not asking him, Do you think crimes should be punished? So my point is in the document where they were these lurid stories, the person who gave the statements was saying that actually you could kill as much as you like and get away with it. I wasn't raising that to say, Oh, is that morally wrong, is that legally wrong, is there a philosophical issue there. My point is that, if this person was saying he could kill as much as he'd like, then that means killing was widespread in the area and that goes to the relevant issues which I mentioned, very specific, relevant issues in Fakovici in that time period. Now, the Prosecution has a frightening, broad-brush approach with the area. I mean, Srebrenica is in one municipality, as I hope we know by now; we're talking about Bratunac municipality. The Prosecution would just merge it all. It's all the same area, it's all the same thing. We need to be precise and specific about dates and times and places. But fundamentally, Your Honour, that was my point. The Prosecution's point is not: Was there impunity on the Bosniak's side, which perhaps is, and I don't know if it's the relevance, not part of their case, but they want to elicit from someone with primary education to tell the Trial Chamber, Do you think crimes should be punished. It's ludicrous. And, in fact, that's why, Your Honour, I really do suspect that the Prosecution wants to get a bloody image on a screen -- I don't know, maybe there's too much publicity going to the Saddam Husein trial and they think they need a bit more in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, for any characterisation of the Prosecution in what I would now say are basically unprofessional terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I really -- it's because I can't imagine any reason why the Prosecution want to get a bloody image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say one last thing. The Prosecution say, Well, we've never objected to lurid images of autopsies. Well, the last one was in closed session, private session when we showed an autopsy. So fine, if the Prosecution are true to that, if they're not seeking publicity or anything else, and if we really must see these images let's see them in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no objection to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, but the whole -- the whole issue is -- you are always in a different position than the Defence, Ms. Sellers, the Prosecution's what I mean. And there's definitely a difference between decapitated civilians or soldiers or fighters being captured and decapitated and others that are beaten up, or tortured, or whatever. I mean, it's still a crime, but certainly what we heard about yesterday, and I'm not saying it's true or not true, I mean it's -- that's beside the point at this stage. Certainly represents something which is more serious than what you wanted to show the witness. I think ultimately the whole issue is the following. Are you aware that such crimes were also committed by Muslims on Serbs? And are you aware of any disciplinary or any other kind of action that was taken against persons who were possibly responsible for these. And you can leave it at that. At the end of the day, I mean, what's going to change if we see an extra video which we have seen already. We haven't seen the decapitated bodies that were mentioned yesterday, but between -- if -- again, because I'm -- don't, please, take me as affirming that what was stated yesterday is being taken by the Trial Chamber as proven, but for argument's sake let's take what was written there -- what was stated by that gentleman in his interviews with that newspaper. It certainly represents something much, much more tragic and much more serious than the -- what we saw on that video, and I don't think you need to show the video, too. But anyway, we'll discuss outside and come back to you with -- because I'm just speaking my own opinion and -- which might change as soon as I hear what my colleagues have to state on the matter. But I think you can still cover the territory without the need of going into other videos. Mr. Jones, you said you also had some other issues to raise this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I think the others can probably wait until the end of the day. There's one housekeeping issue in a way which is we have problems finding the section of the interview which the Prosecution -- sorry, it's a separate issue altogether. When we receive exhibit lists we are having difficult locating both the relevant part of the transcripts and the video portion. We sent an e-mail to the Prosecution last night. Hopefully we'll resolve that. In the meantime, if we -- if I re-examine on the interview, I may need to just read the transcript since that's an exhibit I trust that there's not a -- that there's no objection to that because -- I can explain later if need be, but it's very difficult to find the -- where the transcript matches to the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And there's another one concerning a motion in the case of Drago Nikolic. But I need to mention that before the day is through as well. You may be aware of a motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I am aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We need to -- well, we have a position on that and I want to make Your Honours aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I imagine -- in fact, one of my staff alerted me to that possibility, which I was aware of in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think about this one, the Drago Nikolic, rather than stating it here, I would rather have you put it in writing and formalise it because we have a motion. So if it's formalised it's much better for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will enable us --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just to alert you that we will be filing a motion -- a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was to be expected. I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can imagine why. So can we bring in the witness now? Are there any other issues that you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I would just say from the last -- not the last issue of pleading but the issue of the video, if Your Honours will decide that during the break, I will not by any means be, if allowed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- to use it during the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So just to say that in terms of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- I can --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- the witness could come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we will do it this way. While Madam Usher goes to fetch the witness, we can go out and discuss it. It's not going to take us much time. --- Break taken at 9.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the position, Ms. Sellers, is as follows, that we consider that for the time being you should restrict yourself to asking the basic questions. I'm speak cryptically a little bit --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- for the time being and I'm sure you understand. I think that you should limit yourself initially to the question as to what and to what extent, if at all, he is aware of facts that you have in mind. And you will then make use of that document only if you have a completely negative answer and only if you think that it is useful to use that document with the witness, who ultimately doesn't know who these persons are. Can only look at pictures. So -- but anyway, the approach that we are taking is that this could be handled by simple questions. I think what Mr. Jones said with regard to questions of impunity and not impunity doesn't really arise. It is a question of mere facts, what is we are of. At the end of the day, anything beyond that, it's useless to try and elicit any kind of answer from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I completely understand your ruling and also due to the discretionary nature of the way that we're discussing it now, one response I would have would probably be best made maybe prior to the beginning of the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And as we approach -- as we approach the issue as well. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning to you, Mr. Alic. Again, my apologies to you for keeping you waiting but it happens every day that we have got procedural matters that we need to discuss. So I hope you had time to rest. Today we will be making a humongous effort to finish with your testimony so that you can go back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, and thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are now going to be cross-examined by Ms. Sellers. I suggest to you that you try and keep your answers as concise and to the point as possible so that you would at the end help yourself, too, making it possible to finish in time by the end of business today. Otherwise, if you give lengthy answers you probably end up here tomorrow. Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Alic, and I, too, would like to say thank you very much for your patience. And I do --

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I do hope to finish with your testimony today. I will be asking questions that in the majority will seek to clarify some of the evidence that you've already given to the Trial Chamber. Some of the questions can simply be dealt with as either a "yes" or "no" or "I don't know" answer and the others might call for a brief explanation. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's begin. Mr. Alic, to go back to your background, if I understand correctly that you went to school, elementary school, in Bratunac. And --

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Tell me where you went to elementary school, please.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first four forms in Jagodnja and the second four forms, between the fourth and eighth form, in Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Can you explain to me when you talk about the first four forms, how old were you when you left the end of the first four forms?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry? How old was I --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When you finished the first four forms.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first four, at that point I was 11 years old.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. And then in the second part of your education, sir, in Fakovici, how old were you when you finished that part of your education?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 16, around 16. 16. 11 plus 4 makes 15, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you study any special subjects or areas in this second part of your education?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Special subjects? I'm not quite sure what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would mean subjects to study a technical area, a trade, or a profession.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did a lot of farming. I was helping out my father and my brothers with the machinery and whatever chores needed doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you do your JNA service after you completed your education?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In what year did you do your JNA service?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1989, that's when I began. I was back in 1990, December 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you do your JNA service in the Bratunac area, or did you go to another part of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not the Bratunac area. No barracks there. It was in the surroundings of Belgrade, a place called Pancevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you acquire any special skills when you were in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My specialty in the JNA was anti-air defence. Those were multiple anti-aircraft guns, whole rocket systems that were deployed in case of need. That was positioned where I was, in the same barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you also learn during your JNA service how to activate or deactivate land-mines?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is that something -- is that a skill that you acquired after leaving the JNA service?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, you testified once about deactivating a mine. Was that the first time that you did that or had you learned how to deactivate mines during the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement, that was the first time that I deactivated this mine. Those were the circumstances; I had no choice but to do it. If there's a drowning man, he's likely to be clutching at straws, isn't he? Likewise, I just had to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And can I ask you if your medical skills -- when you became a nurse, was it also in the summer of 1992 the first time that you acquired medical skills?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to concentrate right now on June 1992 and July 1992. You've testified to the Trial Chamber that there was a group of men with you in Jagodnja who formed what were the armed fighters. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Can you tell me who was the oldest man of the group, what was the age of the oldest man of the group?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of age or in terms of something else? In terms of age, I can't remember right now what the respective ages were of the people there, but there were senior people, quite senior in fact, who wanted to defend the land of their forefathers. There were people aged, for example, about 50 who did guard duty who conducted reconnaissance. The situation quite literally was that all of us there had no choice but to defend what was ours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, can you just remind me, is this the group of 10 to 15 men, or now are we talking about a larger group of men?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said between 10 and 15 men who would go to Radijevici, that's if I am not mistaken. You're asking me about the group of people that was in Jagodnja in June and July, so these are two different concepts for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Let's make sure that we're understanding correctly. The group of men who were in Jagodnja in June and July, how many are we talking about in that group who would defend their houses, who would guard Jagodnja?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June a group of people was there and they had weapons, the hunting rifles that I referred to, two rifles from Jagodnja, four from Joseva. And there were different contraptions, makeshift contraptions that we made ourselves, as well as the three automatic rifles that had been seized in the attack in early June. The remaining men had no weapons. There were between 50 and 100 of those civilians, people who had no choice but to join, in order to help in way they could, those people who were in fact in possession of weapons. You couldn't use the same rifles for everybody who had to stand guard around the clock. So we would take turns and we would pass the rifles on. If someone who was actually the owner of a rifle refused to give it to someone else, no one could have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ordered him to give it to someone else by saying, You have to give your rifle to such-and-such a person.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. So am I to understand that there were about 100 men who were performing the guarding of Jagodnja? And this is in June of July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He said between 50 and 100.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Between 50 and 100?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Between 50 and 100. But it wasn't possible for all those people to have weapons because there were no weapons to go around. Those people were involved in defence, if you see my point. Someone produced food, someone worked the fields. We all had to contribute in some way because we had realised that it was our duty to defend our children, our families, and all our possessions. I am specifying what the weapons were that happened to be at our disposal at the time. That's what I'm doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, you've testified that there were many refugees coming into Jagodnja during June and July 1992. I would like to ask you, did any of the male refugees also join this group of between 50 and 100 men that you've just testified -- that you've just spoken about?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There remained some men from Abdulici and Zanjevo. They had their family there. They stayed with their families in order to be able to have sufficient food, but later on they, too, volunteered to be involved in all of the activities. For example, guard duty as well as reconnaissance, especially in the direction of Zanjevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did that make the group of 50 to 100 expand, grow in number, or are we always talking about 50 to 100 men during that period of June and July 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We're still talking about the same figure, and not too many people from Zanjevo survived in the area. Those were people who had moved from Jagodnja to Zanjevo before the war who owned houses, and they -- they had close links with their families, a handful of such people, maybe five or six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment, Ms. Sellers. Is there something wrong with the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's a question of translation of guard duty. Apparently that wasn't actually precisely what he said. It was something more to do with observation duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to clear that up with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, you were talking about what the group of men, the 50 to 100 men did. Could you just clarify with the Trial Chamber, did they at times guard Jagodnja?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From time to time those people would stand guard at night. I'm saying this again. Those six or seven rifles that we had at the time, it's not only the owners of those rifles that could stand guard around the clock. The other people, too, realised that they would have to get involved and stand guard by night. We had night guards. We needed 1.000 people just to cover the area around Jagodnja and Joseva in order to observe or watch the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So did you have a system where the 1.000 people could guard the area, could watch the line, as you've just testified?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please specify what sort of a system you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about a plan. Did you at times have a certain number guard one area with an amount of weapons, maybe another number guard another area, and then -- on the night?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Not that sort of thing. This wasn't something that we could even dream of. It wasn't imaginable. I'm talking about based on my own experience, how it could have been and how it should have been, had we had the manpower and the weapons that were sufficient to protect our village. This was a forested area, and we were in the middle of a forest surrounded by Serb villages on nearly all sides. I'm talking about Jagodnja and Joseva. This is a hilly area, a mountainous area. You have creeks on both sides. You see what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So then let me make sure I'm understanding. Your evidence is that you wished that you had had a thousand men, but that in reality you only had 50 to 100 men who were involved in guarding the area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And that is a mischaracterisation of what he's just said. His answer -- he was asked about a plan, whether there was a place, and he said: No, no, not sort of thing, that wasn't something we could dream of, it wasn't imaginable. He wasn't talking about whether he would like to have had a thousand men, he said whether they would like to have a system, a plan and something organised, and he categorically denied that there was anything like that. It's not this question of manpower, it's a question of whether there's a system.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that goes to one issue. And the other issue is that Mr. Alic said we needed 1.000 people just to cover the area around Jagodnja and Joseva in order to observe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, I think you cannot articulate -- you can actually rephrase because the objection raised by Mr. Jones is perfectly valid. I think you need to rephrase your question, cover the various issues involved or arising out of his previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which, according to you, needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Alic what you're saying is -- are you saying that you wished you'd had a thousand men to guard the area but that you didn't?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a dream. When we were expelled from Srebrenica and reached Tuzla, when we tried to sum up the whole situation, that would have been our only option of opposing the sort of force that was attacking us. I'm not sure if that's a satisfactory answer for you; if not, then we can move on to a different issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask again about how you guarded?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Sellers. Because with the system, how it operates, I'm just trying to attract your attention that your client wanted to hand a paper to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, let's go back to how you did guard. Am I correct in understanding that there was no plan, there was no system, in guarding the village?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no plan, there was no system, nothing to suggest how it should work. One stood guard where there were people who had fled Joseva and the refugees who were in the forest. That's where people stood guard, around those places.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with this group of 50 to 100 men, was Asim Smajlovic the leader of this group?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Asim Smajlovic, that he was the leader of that group in Jagodnja, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So he was a leader of the group that you've just described of between the 50 to 100 men. That's your testimony, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 50 to 100 men, these men were unarmed. I'm saying that they only assisted in night guards. The group of men that had weapons was a different group at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. And that's what I'm trying to understand. Was Asim Smajlovic only the leader of the group of the 15 men, or was he also the leader of the group of the 50 to 100 men?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Asim Smajlovic was the leader only of those men who had weapons, those 15 men who volunteered to stand guard. The others also volunteered. Those who had families in the camp, they felt duty-bound to stand guard. Asim could not have ordered anyone to stand guard or not stand guard. There were only about 15 men who were involved and who voluntarily wished to perform some sort of tasks. There were people who went to reconnoitre in the direction of Fakovici to watch the situation towards Fakovici. It was very dangerous to go there, and they volunteered to do so. Asim was the leader of those people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. So, Mr. Alic, Asim was the leader of the men who had weapons. Is that correct? I just want to take this step by step to make sure I'm --

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And so, within these men, these 15 men with weapons, they would sometimes reconnoitre or do reconnaissance or observation of places outside of Jagodnja?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And you, as a nurse, worked or assisted Asim Smajlovic to make sure if any of these 15 men were wounded or injured in any way would receive medical care. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, in June and July, those 15 men never went in that direction all together. It would be two or three of them who would go with binoculars to the spots I showed on the map to observe the movements of the Serb soldiers. That was the aim, to observe the movements of Serb soldiers to avoid murders happening as had happened in May and early June.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, were you aware of what Mr. Smajlovic did with the information that was brought back by the people who were observing with the binoculars? Did he pass it on to someone?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. There was no one for him to pass it on to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did he inform the refugees or the people within the village of the information from the reconnaissance?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear him informing the refugees in the village of that. In my view, there would have been no logic in that. If he didn't tell me, why would he tell a refugee? But I don't know that, really. I don't believe that Asim Smajlovic informed a refugee of that. But the people who were going in the direction of Fakovici, Zanjevo to get food would be warned that there were large numbers of soldiers moving around in the woods, that mines had been laid in the woods. So it was those people who were told.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alic, you testified that during the summer of 1992 a man, Mr. Alic, came from Srebrenica. He was originally from Abdulici, but he came to your area. My question is: Were you aware of whether people in Srebrenica were concerned about the -- the defence of Jagodnja?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question. It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Let me ask it in this manner. Were you aware yourself or the group that you were with, with Mr. Smajlovic, were you aware that people in Srebrenica were concerned, were worried, about the inhabitants and the refugees in Jagodnja?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't know about that, that somebody was concerned about us, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that the Trial Chamber and Mr. Alic, Defence, watch the first Prosecution video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Which exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It is P328. And the transcript -- it's the Word transcript, tape 4, pages 14 through 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, I'm going to ask you to watch this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: "Naser ORIC: So the commanders of the various villages which make up the area of Potocari didn't want to obey him, they wanted to obey me. And basically everybody was doing his own thing."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would like you to stop -- I want to stop here for the time being. It's difficult for us, and I would imagine it's even worse for the witness, who is the person who is talking here on the video referring to? Who is he referring to? Because I think we started the video from a part -- from a section which does not give us an indication as to who he is referring to. I mean, I can't understand who he is referring to, although I can guess, having seen this video before. But I'm just relying on my memory, which sometimes plays tricks on me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, are you referring to where it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We started from a section where obviously the interviewee is referring to someone, but we have no indication as to who that someone is --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if you start --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- just a few seconds before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly we can. I can say who it is. I don't believe it's necessarily relevant to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We would object to any evidence being given about who is speaking or who he is referring to. And we also -- there's no time frame either. If we can play the video so we have some time frame, otherwise the witness has no idea what time is being spoken of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The time frame --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The year, the month, otherwise how is he supposed to answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can give a description of what the time frame is speaking about, but I thought that it would be best if the content in the video --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is this: I don't know what your question is going to be because I --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It does not relate to the reference of that person. I will tell you that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And it's just for a sake of where we had begun, but I'm more than willing to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't -- any description by the Prosecution of the context of this -- of what we're about to see, any description of the time frame that's being covered, it's all completely contended -- contentious on our part and unless the video speaks for itself as to what time frame, I would object to any witness -- any question being put to this witness which suggests a time frame, which suggests 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994, unless it's clear from the video. We certainly don't want the Prosecution giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise we would have to see the whole video, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's precisely it, though. To have a witness shown a chunk of a video which he has no idea what was said before, what was said afterwards, and then to get him -- an answer from him, we'll get completely misleading evidence from him, and so we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- absolutely object. Either the whole video is to be shown or the Prosecution has to find some other way of dealing with it. But we're certainly not going to accept that the Prosecution can say, All right, in this section this is being described and this is the time period, and what do you say about it, because we simply don't accept that there's any specific time period, we don't accept any description the Prosecution is giving. It's not for them to interpret what's being said, it's for them only to play what appears to be being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know what the question is going to be, Mr. Jones. Why you seem to know? I would imagine you don't know either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, already it's clear that the question is going to be -- well, I'll wait. If the question suggests a time frame --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- I mean, I stopped the running of the video because, since it started with obviously a reference to some unnamed individual, I wanted to make sure that if there are going to be questions on that individual that the witness hears the entire section from the video. But if you're telling me that that part is irrelevant, I don't know why we are starting from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was just a question of editing, and I did not intend to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go ahead and see what the question is and then we'll decide accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "Naser ORIC: [Interpretation] So the commanders of the various villages which make up the area of Potocari didn't want to obey him, they only wanted to obey me and basically everybody was doing their own thing. "But I managed to just convince them to solve the situation this way, that I convinced them that I had to be at the central HQ in Srebrenica, but that I would come to Potocari very often and see how things were and how things run there. "So we made a kind of improvised centre, an improvised HQ, a centre there in the Domavija. And then we -- we had to get in contact with some of the village -- some of the other outlying villages such as Ljeskovik, that's L-j -- L-j-e-s-k-o-v-i-k, Klotjevac, K-l-o-t-j-e-v-a-c Prohici, P-r-o-h-i-c-i, Skejici, S-k-e-j-i-c-i, Osatica, O-s-a-t-i-c-a, and Radjenovici, R-a-d-j-e-n-o-v-i-c-i, Karacica Brdo, that's Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. K-a-r-a-c-i-c-a, one word, and then Brdo, B-r-d-o, Greben, G-r-e-b-e-n, Karacici, another village, K-a-r-c-i-c-i, and also with the villages of Osmace, which we had before, Mursalovici, that's M-u-r-s-a-l-o-v-i-c-i, Gecimici, that's G-e-c-i-m-i-c-i, and then also with the villages of Podkorjen, that's P-o-d-k-o-r-j-e-n, and then also with the villages of Podkorjen, that's P-o-d-k-o-r-j-e-n and then Tokoljaci, T-o-k-o-l-j-a-c-i, Jagodnja, that's J-a-g-o-d-n-j-a. "All of these villages that we've listed were all separated, they were all in their own little enclaves. So, for example, Jagodnja and Joseva, this was one enclave which was completely surrounded by Chetniks. And there was another enclave, Pozarovci [phoen], Podkorjen, and Miholjevo [phoen] which was again one enclave surrounded by Chetniks. Osmace was another enclave where also the village of Gecimici and Mursalovici were. And then there were another enclave consisted of Tokoljaci, Mehmedovici, and Mosici [phoen]. And yet another enclave consisting of Knezovici, Karacici, and Greben. And then there was another larger enclave consisting of Glodovici [phoen], Crni Vrh, Glojvici [phoen], Skelici, and Osatica. "We sent couriers to these villages, asking them to send us someone from each of these villages to tell us how many weapons they had, how many fighters they had, so that we could also organise the visits in these enclaves as well. "They were -- they were in the process. They had already organised themselves and were in the process of cleaning out the area between the various enclaves so that they would then be connected between themselves. "In the meantime, Hakija Meholjic who he sent Akif to establish contact with these villages, he had the task of going to these enclaves, to see what they were doing, what needed to be done, but they were very often blockaded by the Chetniks. So they would hide, together with this group of armed men, in the forests. "That day when all of these -- that day when all of these various enclaves became connected together and became one entity, a couple of the representatives from these villages came, they didn't all want to come, but some of them came. "They had -- they had decided amongst -- they had themselves decided that their commander would be Sefik Mandzic, that's S-e-f-i-k M-a-n-d-z-i-c. Apart from the Biljeg Territorial Defence where the commander was Akmo Tihic -- and the commander there was Ahmo Tihic, who was working independently in the area from Biljeg toward Jagodnja down toward Skelani. He didn't want to go into -- he didn't want to go into part of the Osat Territorial Defence, because he wanted to collect all the other things together and to make a Skelani Territorial Defence."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, would you confirm what was said about Jagodnja and Joseva occurred, that they were surrounded, became an enclave?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well -- we need a time period, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the next clause I'm about to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but, I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- you can include it in one question and say, Do you confirm that any time Jagodnja and Joseva became, what time would that be.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to confirm that his testify, I think Mr. Alic already testified and I'd like to know, yes, does this confirm that Joseva and Jagodnja became surrounded by a Serb enclave in the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's the danger of does this confirm, because as we said this doesn't provide a time frame. If he -- if the witness says -- or he's already said it was surrounded in some other time frame and doesn't confirm what's being said if it's a different time frame which has been referred to. She can ask the question, Ms. Sellers, but it's not confirming what was said here unless we're -- unless the time frames are identical. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think this is a storm in a teacup. Basically, it can be dealt with to an ad hoc, direct question which you are entitled to on cross-examination in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, wasn't Jagodnja and Joseva -- excuse me, Joseva surrounded by Serbs in 1992 as of May, June, and July, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Alic, wasn't Ahmo Tihic working in the Biljeg area or active in the Biljeg area in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Ahmo was doing at Biljeg, but I do know that there was a wood between Biljeg and Jagodnja which was not controlled by either Ahmo Tihic or us. There were ambushes set up there by the Serb army, and I don't remember whether Ahmo Tihic came to Jagodnja on one or two occasions or not. In the area between Jagodnja and Biljeg, we hid in creeks in order to get to Biljeg and it went on like this until 1993. I said all that yesterday. In 1993, the Serbs cut off this corridor we could use to pass through. And three of our men were killed in Ravni Hrg. You can see that on the map and that can be explained.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Alic, to your knowledge wasn't Ahmo Tihic defending, fighting, or acting in a military manner in that wood in Biljeg in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I said, he was at Biljeg. But from what side the Chetniks or the Serb soldiers were coming, they could only have come from the direction of Skelani and that part overlooking Jagodnja, the wood, they could enter and act there. It means that they were attacking Ahmo at Biljeg, but we stayed in Jagodnja and Joseva. You can see that on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And then I have one other question to ask in relationship to this video. It speaks about Osmace. And didn't you go to Osmace in the summer of 1992, when you were receiving -- when you received training as a nurse?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In early June when there was the attack on Jagodnja and Joseva I went in the direction of Osmace.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And was Osmace also a community that was under attack or had been attacked by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I entered the village of Murselovici, that's the first village in the direction of Osmace. It's called Murselovici. I found that cousin of mine there, and they explained to me how I was to proceed. Not to go towards the village of Brezani from where they were firing, from Jezero and those parts shells were arriving. All the windows were boarded up there because of the daily shelling of Osmace and there were snipers from a hill called Suljanovo Brdo [phoen] and we went through creeks in the wood and it took us a long time to get there from Jagodnja.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So we're about to come up on the break and I want to ask you very quickly: Would you agree with what this video, what is being said in this video, about Jagodnja and Joseva in 19 -- in summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to be -- I -- you need to be precise. I mean, what --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you agree with this video --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because it says more than one thing. So go through the list of the things that it says and --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you agree, therefore, what this video says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- that was -- going to be your objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- about Jagodnja and Joseva being encircled, surrounded in an enclave in the summer of 1992? Yes or no, please. I'm sorry, the answer wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't think he got our entire question or understood your question. You need to repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, do you -- would you say that what the video said about Jagodnja and Joseva being surrounded confirms what you've testified about to this Trial Chamber, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jagodnja and Joseva were surrounded on all sides by Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you also agree that what you've testified about Osmace is in agreement with how the video characterises Osmace as also having been isolated or surrounded?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Osmace, I can't say anything about that because I entered Osmace from one side and I saw those beams that had been set up, or rather the boards on the house windows because they were afraid of shells. But whether it was surrounded on the other sides, I can't confirm that because I didn't go there. I didn't go all the way around Osmace.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarity. And my last question is then: Would you confirm that what this video has said in terms of Ahmo Tihic being in the Biljeg region is correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Here -- one moment before you answer. Because here I have to draw your attention to the fact that the video does not just say that Ahmo Tihic operated in the Biljeg area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It says several things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but it's -- also indicates that he was operating also in a particular direction also in relation to Jagodnja and Joseva. So I think there are at least three things that I recollect from what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think you have to ask him a specific question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to go -- expand that part in the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I wanted to see if he would recognise -- if he agrees that Ahmo Tihic was operating in the Biljeg region in the summer of 1992. Would you agree with that, as stated on the video? Just that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In this case, let him answer first because it's an innocuous --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Ahmo Tihic -- I learned about Ahmo Tihic in Biljeg in late July, that he was there with his group of men. What he was doing and where he was going, I really don't know and in what direction he was acting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That confirms exactly what he said -- what he testified earlier on. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It seemed that it was being suggested in the video it was being suggested that there was a time frame of 1992 and that's my continuing objection. I don't want it to be suggested that the video is referring to any time frame because it is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's have a break, a 25-minute break, starting from now, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's continue. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because my monitor has gone black and I notice that yours is black, too. Yeah, it's okay. It's come now. All right. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, you testified that you went to the woods to where Ahmo Tihic's camp was along with Asim Smajlovic in the summer of 1992. My question is: When you went on those two occasions, did you know whether Mr. Tihic had a commander that was superior to him?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you know whether Mr. Tihic acted together with other commanders in the region?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know or did you know that summer whether Mr. Tihic ever went to Srebrenica for meetings with other commanders?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to show Mr. Alic a second video, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which one -- is it 329 now?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's 329 -- I'm sorry, it's P328.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tape 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It's tape 3, page 15 to 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, please watch the video on your screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: "Naser ORIC: [Interpretation] After I was elected to be a commander, in practice I was basically the same as I had been before. There was still the Territorial Defence units and I was still the commander of the Territorial Defence units. And in practice I stayed a soldier, as I had been before. At that meeting, we agreed that Ahmo Tihic, who was also a member of the HQ, and up until then had been -- and up until then, that is up until the formation of the HQ, he had been a member of the Territorial Defence in Suceska. And he was born in the village of Skelani, right by the bridge that goes over towards Bajina Basta. And because he had been an activist in the SDA party -- before the -- before the -- some police station had been formed in Skelani, the Serbs created a -- sorry, the Serbs drove the local police there out and formed their own municipality there. And just -- the very formation of the Serbian municipality of Skelani meant that all the SDA activists in the area had to leave, had to flee, and if they didn't flee, they were captured. The Chetniks were mostly interested in Ahmo Tihic because he was very active before the war in the SDA party and they considered him an extremist. And then so he with his brother and some relatives there together with some weapons that they had bought before the war illegally, I don't know exactly how but this way or the other. Later on they fled from Skelani to the Territorial Defence in Suceska."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, you testified that the Skelani municipality was created in 1992. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And you also testified that Mr. Ahmo Tihic was someone who was politically active in 1992. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ahmo Tihic had been active since 1991 when the SDA was founded, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was Ahmo Tihic known within the Skelani region as someone who was an activist and someone who would defend Muslims against the Serb-created municipality?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Ahmo Tihic as a farmer and a very wealthy man. I know that he was a member of the SDA. As for the other things you've mentioned, I never heard anything about him being an extremist; this is not something that I'm familiar with. Once in 1991 he came to our place to get some cattle, and that's when I got to know him. I hadn't known him before this time. The distance between us and him was between 15 and 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, when you visited Ahmo Tihic with Asim Smajlovic in the summer of 1992, did you notice whether he had any weapons with him in the woods?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were with Ahmo Tihic, Ahmo had no weapons at all. He was with two other men. There were the two of us, Asim and myself, and another three men from Jagodnja and Joseva. We found him in the middle of the woods sitting at a table. That's something I explained yesterday. But he was not carrying a weapon, not that I noticed. Perhaps he'd left it behind before he met him. But certainly at the moment when we saw him, he was not carrying a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And can I ask you whether you knew whether Mr. Ahmo Tihic had bought or sold weapons illegally in 1992, before the war?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, Mr. Alic, you testified that you've lived in Jagodnja and in the Joseva region all your life and you knew all of the people who lived there. I would like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you: Do you know a Hasib Kurtic, Hasib Kurtic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Hasib Kurtic. We're the same generation and we went to school together, if we're talking about the same person because there's another Hasib at Joseva. So this might be a person from a different locality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, this person -- I'm asking of people who you knew who could come from other Jagodnja or Joseva. I'm asking now do you know a Dzenad Bektic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the name for me. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dzenad Bektic.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dzenad, no. There's no person called Dzenad in our village, no. Dzenad, that's not a name that I'm familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Maybe in Joseva?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dzenad in Joseva, no. There's no such name there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know Fahrudin Avdic or did you know? I'm talking about during the war.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fahrudin Avdic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you know a Ferid Bektic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And Ahmed Alic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mirzet Kurtic, Mirzet Kurtic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirzet, yes. Mirzet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The people's name who I've read with the exception of Dzezad -- Dzenad Bektic, are these people that lived in Jagodnja and Joseva?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm speaking of 1992 to 1995, let's say the period of the war.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many people from Jagodnja and Joseva whose houses had burned down in mid-May, that period of time. And they would go to the nearby villages to seek out their families. People who had gotten married in one of the neighbour villages or maybe they had an aunt there, so that's where people went. Specifically, some came back to our village and some would go, stay for a short while, and come back again to our area, Jagodnja and Joseva.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I might for purposes of expediency, as Defence counsel did yesterday, I would just refer the Trial Chamber to the census under D840 to say that the names we have gone through are on the census in terms of Joseva. And I hope that that will just accelerate a bit of the examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Alic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have a problem with that, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, it's just that there was a question asked about whether those people were living in Jagodnja and Joseva in 1992, and that actually hasn't been answered. And so there's going to be an ambiguity. The census is before the war --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Might I state -- should I rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were they from that area. I believe that is what the census question that was posed by Defence yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alic, I would like to ask you, when you went into the Biljeg woods and you saw Mr. Ahmo Tihic, were you able to see whether they had -- whether Mr. Tihic and his men had any food?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't linger there. I don't know whether they had any food or not, and they certainly didn't tell us whether they had any food or not and we didn't ask. I told you the reason why Ahmo Tihic had invited us to come to Biljeg.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like Mr. Alic now to see an extremely brief video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which one is this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is P433. There is no transcript. There is nothing -- basically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We got notice of this this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
